Thereupon he accepted it and wore it.
Fótúchéng traveled with the various Shí clan members.
The *Separate Biography of Chéng* says:
"The Daoist Fótúchéng,
I do not know from where he came,
came from Dūnhuáng,
loved Buddhism,
and became a renunciate monk.
During the Yǒngjiā period,
he arrived in Luòyáng.
Encountering difficulties in the capital,
he hid in the wilderness.
Hearing that Shí Lè was valiant, extraordinary and fond of killing,
he used Lè's general Guō Mò to briefly see Lè.
He used sesame oil to smear his palm,
to predict good and bad fortune.
From hundreds of *lǐ* away, he could hear the bell of the Buddhist temple,
and foreknow misfortune and fortune.
Lè greatly respected and trusted him.
When Hǔ ascended the throne,
he also took Chéng as his teacher,
and called him the Great Monk.
He knew the day of his death.
When his coffin was opened, there was no corpse,
Only the kāshāya monastic robes and dharma garments remained.
Lín Gōng said:
"Chéng regarded Shí Hǔ as a seagull."
The *Book of Zhào* says:
"Hǔ’s courtesy name was Jìlóng,
he was Lè’s cousin.
In his campaigns, he always beheaded generals and seized flags.
When Lè died,
he executed all of Lè’s sons
and usurped the throne."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"There was a man who lived by the sea who loved seagulls.
Every morning, he went to the sea
and played with the seagulls.
Hundreds of seagulls would come and not leave.
His father said:
'I heard that the seagulls play with you,
catch some and bring them back for us to play with.'
The next day, he went to the sea,
but the seagulls danced and would not come down."
Xiè Rénzǔ, at the age of eight,
(was) the son of Xiè Yùzhāng Kūn,
(and was) remarkably perceptive.
When seeing off guests,
ěrshí yǔ yǐ shéngwù, (at that time his speech already demonstrated understanding,)
and he naturally mingled with the upper class.
Everyone sighed in admiration, saying:
"Yán Huí, at a young age, sat with dignity."
Rénzǔ said:
"Without Ní Fù present,
how can one distinguish Yán Huí?"
The *Jìn Yáng Qiū* says:
"Xiè Shàng, zi Rénzǔ,
was a native of Chén Commandery,
the son of Kūn.
In childhood, he mourned the loss of his elder brother,
his grief surpassing that of others.
When he encountered his father's death,
Wēn Qiào offered condolences,
Shàng's cries were exceedingly sorrowful.
Afterwards, he wiped away his tears and spoke,
showing himself to be an extraordinary child.
Qiào marveled at him,
and from this he became known,
eventually serving as General Who Pacifies the West and
Governor of Yù Province."
When Táo Gōng was critically ill,
he offered no words of advice or suggestion,
which the court officials considered regrettable.
The *Táo shì xù* says:
"Kǎn, zi Shìhéng,
his ancestors were from Póyáng,
later moving to Xúnyáng.
From a young age, Kǎn had lofty ambitions to govern and maintain the universe.
When he was recommended as Xiàolián and entered Luòyáng,
the Sīkōng Zhāng Huá saw him and said,
"In the future, one who will assist the ruler and bring peace to the people,
that person is you."
Liú Hóng, while garrisoned in Miǎn Nán,
took him as Chief Clerk,
and said to Kǎn,
"In the past, when I served as an assistant to Grand Tutor Yáng,
I heard him say,
'You will later occupy this very position.'
Now, observing you,
it seems that it is so again."
He was successively promoted to Inspector of the Xiāng,
Guǎng, and Jīng three provinces,
granted feathered canopy and ceremonial music,
enfeoffed as Duke of Chángshā Commandery,
and Great General.
When attending court he was not called by name,
and he was allowed to carry swords and wear shoes on the palace steps.
He was posthumously promoted to Grand Commandant,
and granted the title of Grand Marshal,
with the posthumous name Huán Gōng."
According to Wáng Yǐn's *Jin Shu*, Kǎn's deathbed memorial stated:
"I grew up as an orphan in poverty,
and my initial aspirations were limited.
I have received extraordinary favor from past generations of the preceding dynasty.
I am almost eighty years old,
and have reached the highest position a subject can attain.
I can move my hands and feet,
what more should I regret!
Only because the remaining bandits have not been exterminated,
and the imperial tombs have not been recovered,
therefore I feel both indignant and concerned,
and that is all!
I still hope that my old age, like that of a dog or horse,
can be prolonged a little,
and I wish to swallow Shí Hǔ to the north for Your Majesty,
and execute Lǐ Xióng to the west,
but my strength has failed,
and my good plans are forever extinguished.
As I face the writing, I shake my wrists,
tears and mucus flow down my face.
I humbly request that you carefully select a replacement for me,
ensuring that you find a truly capable person,
sufficient to uphold and proclaim the royal plans,
and complete my unfinished aspirations.
Then, though it be the day of my death,
it will feel like the year of my birth."
If there is a memorial like this,
it is not without advice and suggestions.
Emperor Rénzǔ heard this and said:
"Because there is no Shù Diāo in this era,
I will not leave behind the words of Lord Táo."
《Lǚ Shì Chūn Qiū》 says:
"Guǎn Zhòng was ill,
Duke Huán asked:
"If you, Master, should not recover,
who will replace you as the Chancellor?
What about Shù Diāo?"
Guǎn Zhòng said,
"To castrate oneself in order to serve the ruler
is against human nature;
he must not be employed!"
Later, he indeed caused chaos in Qí."
The worthies of the time considered this a virtuous saying.
Zhú Fǎshēn was at Emperor Jiǎnwén's seat when
Liú Yǐn asked,
"Why does the Daoist priest frequent the red gate?"
He replied,
"You yourself see it as a red gate;
to this poor priest, it is like wandering in a thatched hut."
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* says,
"The Dharma Master resided in Kuàijī.
The Emperor valued his moral character
and sent envoys to welcome him.
The Dharma Master briefly came out to respond to the command.
The Sītú (Minister Over the Masses) and Prince of Kuàijī was naturally indifferent and serene,
and formed a warm friendship with the Dharma Master.
Although the Master ascended the red steps
and entered and exited the red mansion,
he remained indifferent and broad-minded,
no different than being in a thatched hut."
Some say it was Biàn Lìng.
Different accounts.
Sūn Shèng 孫盛 served as Yǔ Gōng's 庾公 (Yǔ Liàng 庾亮) Record Keeper and Military Advisor.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" 《中興書》 says:
"Shèng's 盛 courtesy name was Ānguó 安國.
He was from Zhōngdū 中都, Tàiyuán 太原.
He was learned and had a strong memory.
He successively held the positions of Compiler and
Magistrate of Liúyáng 瀏陽.
When Yǔ Liàng 庾亮 became the Governor of Jīngzhōu 荊州,
he appointed him as Chief Secretary of the Expedition to the West,
and he was promoted to Secretary of the Imperial Secretariat."
Once, on a hunting trip,
he brought his two sons along.
Yǔ Gōng 庾公 was unaware of this.
Suddenly, he saw Qízhuāng 齊莊 in the hunting grounds.
At that time, he was seven or eight years old.
Yǔ 庾 said to him:
"So, you've come too?"
He immediately replied:
"As it is said,
'Neither small nor great,
we follow the Duke in his progress.'"
When Sūn Qíyóu 孫齊由 and Sūn Qízhuāng 孫齊莊 were young, they went to see Yǔ Gōng 庾公.
Yǔ Gōng 庾公 asked:
"What is Qíyóu's 齊由 courtesy name?"
He replied:
"His courtesy name is Qíyóu."
The Duke said:
"Whom does he wish to emulate?"
He said:
"He emulates Xǔ Yóu."
The *Jìn Bǎiguān Míng* says:
"Sūn Qián's courtesy name was Qíyóu,
a native of Tàiyuán."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Qián was
the eldest son of Shèng.
When Yùzhāng Prefect Ŷn Zhòngkān was sent to punish Wáng Guóbǎo,
Qián was at that time in the commandery,
and was forced to be a consultative military advisor,
but he firmly declined and did not accept,
and subsequently died of grief."
"What is Qí Zhuāng's courtesy name?"
He replied:
"His courtesy name is Qízhuāng."
The Duke said:
"Whom does he wish to emulate?"
He said:
"He emulates Zhuāng Zhōu."
The Duke said:
"Why not admire Zhòng Ní but admire Zhuāng Zhōu?"
He replied:
"The sage is born with knowledge,
gù nán qǐ mù." Therefore, it is difficult to aspire to emulating them."
Yǔ Gōng dàxǐ xiǎo'ér duì. "Yǔ Gōng was greatly pleased with the child's response."
《Sūn Fàng Bié Zhuàn》 yuē: "The *Biography of Sūn Fàng* says:"
"Fàng zì Qízhuāng, "Fàng's courtesy name was Qízhuāng,"
jiān jūn cìzǐ yě. "He was the second son of Jiān Jūn."
nián bā suì, "At the age of eight,"
tàiwèi Yǔ Gōng zhàojiàn zhī. "Grand Commandant Yǔ Gōng summoned him for an audience."
Fàng qīngxiù, "Fàng was refined and handsome,"
yù guān shì, "Wanting to observe his talent,"
nǎi shòu zhǐ bǐ lìng shū, "He then gave him paper and brush, ordering him to write,"
Fàng biàn zì shū míngzì. "Fàng readily wrote his own name."
Gōng tí hòu wèn zhī yuē: "Gōng wrote a question after it, asking:"
"Wèi yù mù Zhuāng Zhōu xié?" "Is it that you wish to emulate Zhuāng Zhōu?"
Fàng shū dá yuē: "Fàng wrote in reply:"
"Yì yù mù zhī." "I intend to emulate him."
Gōng yuē: "Gōng said:"
"Hé gù bù mù Zhòng Ní ér mù Zhuāng Zhōu?" "Why do you not emulate Zhòng Ní but emulate Zhuāng Zhōu?"
Fàng yuē: "Fàng said:"
"Zhòng Ní shēng ér zhī zhī, "Zhòng Ní was born with knowledge,"
fēi xī qǐ suǒ jí; "Not attainable by aspiring after it;"
zhìyú Zhuāng Zhōu, "As for Zhuāng Zhōu,"
shì qí cì zhě, "He is second to him,"
gù mù ěr." "Therefore, I emulate him."
Gōng wèi bīnkè yuē: "Gōng said to his guests:"
"Wáng Fǔsì yìng dá, "Even if Wáng Fǔsì were to respond,"
kǒng bùnéng shèng zhī." "I fear he would not be able to surpass him."
zú Chángshā Wáng xiāng." "He eventually became the Chancellor of the King of Chángshā."
Zhāng Xuánzhī and
Gù Fū
were both maternal grandsons of Gù Hé.
Both were intelligent and wise from a young age.
Hé knew both of them,
but he always said Gù was superior.
His affection and attention were particularly inclined towards him,
which Zhāng greatly resented.
Fū was treated differently.
*Xù Jìn Yángqiū* states:
"Zhāng Xuánzhī, zi Zǔxī,
was the grandson of Chéngzhī, the Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
He became known for his learning at a young age.
He successively held the position of Minister of Personnel,
and was later appointed General of the Championing Army
and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Xiè Xuán, the Intendant of Huìjī, arrived at his commandery at the same time.
Commentators considered them to be the hope of the North and South.
Xuánzhī's reputation was second only to Xiè Xuán.
At the time, they were also known as the Two Xuáns of the North and South.
He died in his commandery."
At that time, Zhāng was nine years old,
and Gù was seven years old.
Hé brought them both to a temple.
Seeing the image of the Buddha's *nirvana*,
some disciples were weeping,
while others were not.
Hé asked his two grandsons about it.
Xuán said,
"Weeping for deceased relatives and friends,
not weeping for those who are not relatives or friends."
Fū said:
"That is not so,
it should be because one has forgotten emotions that one does not weep,
it is because one cannot forget emotions that one weeps."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* says:
"The Buddha entered Parinirvana between the shade of the Sala trees,
lying with his head to the north,
the earth shook greatly.
All who were learning the three studies,
universally felt unhappy,
mournfully intermingling their tears.
All those who had learned nothing more,
only contemplated the dharma,
that everything is impermanent."
Yǔ Fǎchǎng visited Yǔ Tàiwèi,
holding a duster that was extremely fine,
the duke said:
"This is extremely fine,
how did you obtain it?"
Fǎchǎng said:
"The honest do not seek it,
the greedy are not given it,
therefore I obtained it."
The origin of Fǎchǎng's clan is not known in detail.
Fǎ Chǎng wrote the "Rén Wù Lùn" (Commentary on Personalities),
and in his self-description, he praised himself, saying:
"His comprehension is sharp and insightful,
and his talent for language is fluent and eloquent."
Yǔ Zhìgōng served as the governor of Jīngzhōu.
The "Yǔ Yì Bié Zhuàn" (Separate Biography of Yǔ Yì) states:
"Yì's courtesy name was Zhìgōng.
He was from Yānlíng in Yǐngchuān.
He possessed great magnanimity from a young age,
and contemporary opinion held him capable of grand strategy.
After his elder brother, the Grand Commandant Liàng, passed away,
the court discussed and recommended talent,
and consequently, Yì was appointed as the commander-in-chief of seven provinces.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the South
and Governor of Jīngzhōu."
He presented a feather fan to Emperor Wǔ.
Emperor Wǔ suspected it was an old object.
Fù Xián's "Yǔ Shàn Fù Xù" (Preface to the Rhapsody on Feather Fans) states:
"In the past, the people of Wú simply cut bird wings and waved them.
The wind produced by the two round or square fans did not diminish,
nor was their effectiveness increased.
Yet, in the Central Kingdom, no one had the idea of making them.
After the subjugation of Wú,
everyone suddenly valued them,
and there was no one who did not use them."
According to records, Yǔ Yì presented a white feather fan to Emperor Wǔ,
but the emperor disliked it for not being new
Conversely,
he was not heard of again.
The Attendant Liú Shào said:
The "Treatise on Writing" says:
"Shào's courtesy name was Yànzǔ,
a native of Cóngtíng in Péngchéng.
His grandfather was Nà,
the Chief Commandant of the Capital Province.
His father was Sōng,
the Magistrate of Chénggāo.
Shào was learned and fond of study,
possessed many talents,
and was skilled in cursive and clerical script.
He initially served as a military advisor to the Commander-in-Chief,
when the Grand Tutor went east,
Shào believed that the capital Luoyang would be in danger,
so he rode alone to Yángzhōu.
He successively served as Attendant,
and Governor of Yùzhāng."
"For the cloud-high structure of the Bǎiliáng Palace,
the craftsmen first resided beneath it;
for the intricate performance of wind and string instruments,
Zhōng and Kuí first listened to their sound.
Zhōng refers to Zhōng Qī.
Kuí was the music master of Emperor Shùn.
To present an old fan [to the emperor],
is for quality, not for novelty."
Lady Yǔ heard this and said:
"Cǐ rén yí zài dì zuǒyòu."
After Hé Piàojì (何驃騎) died,
Hé Chōng (何充) held a separate audience.
He summoned Gōng Zhǔ (褚公) to enter.
After he arrived at Shítóu (石頭),
Wáng Chángshǐ (王長史)
and Liú Yǐn (劉尹) went together to visit Zhǔ (褚).
Zhǔ (褚) said,
"How does Zhēn Cháng (真長) intend to place me?"
Zhēn Cháng (真長) turned to Wáng (王) and said,
"This fellow is eloquent."
Zhǔ (褚) then looked at Wáng (王),
and Wáng (王) said,
"The state already has a Duke of Zhou."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* (晉陽秋) says:
"When Chōng (充) died,
the discussants said that the Empress Dowager's father, Póu (裒), should be in charge of the government.
Póu (裒) entered the court from Dāntú (丹徒).
The Minister of Personnel, Liú Xiá (劉遐), advised Póu (裒), saying,
'The King of Kuàijī (會稽王) is virtuous
and is the Duke of Zhou of the state.
Your Excellency should entrust him with the great affairs of state.'
Póu's (裒) Chief Clerk, Wáng Húzhī (王胡之), also advised him to return to his fief,
and so he firmly declined and returned to the capital."
When Huán Gōng (桓公) was on a northern expedition and passed through Jīnchéng (金城),
he saw the willows he had planted when he was previously in Lángyá (琅邪),
They were all already ten spans in circumference.
He sighed and said:
"The trees are still like this,
how can men endure it!"
He climbed the branches and held onto the twigs,
tears streaming down his face.
"The Unofficial Biography of Huán Wēn" says:
"Wēn's courtesy name was Yuánzǐ,
he was from Lóngkàng in the Qiáo state,
a descendant of Huán Róng, the Fifth Watchman of the Hàn Dynasty.
His father, Yí,
had insightful judgment.
Wēn had a bold and unrestrained spirit from a young age,
and was known to Wēn Qiào.
He was repeatedly promoted to Intendant of Lángyé,
and then promoted to Great General Who Conquers the West,
stationed in Western Xià.
At that time, the rebellious Hú had not yet been exterminated,
and the remaining embers were falsely extinguished.
Wēn personally commanded the soldiers of the commandery,
raised the banner and launched expeditions to suppress them,
clearing and sweeping Yī and
Luò, displaying respect at the imperial tombs.
He died, and was posthumously named Marquis Xuānwǔ."
When Jiǎnwén was serving as Commander of the Army,
he once entered the court with Huán Xuānwǔ,
and they yielded the right of way to each other.
Xuānwǔ, unable to hold back, went ahead of him.
Thereupon he said,
"Bóyě grasps the shū,
leading the way for the king."
This is from the *Book of Odes* of Wèi.
The shū is twelve feet long
and has no blade.
Jiǎnwén said,
"This is what is meant by
'Neither small nor great,
Following the Duke on his march.'"
Gù Yuè was the same age as Jiǎnwén,
but his hair turned white early.
The *Zhongxing Shu* says:
"Yuè's courtesy name was Jūnshū,
and he was from Jìnlíng.
He initially served as Yin Hao's Assistant Officer of Yángzhōu.
After Hao died,
he submitted a memorial arguing on Hao's behalf.
Someone advised him that because Hao was dismissed by Emperor Tàizōng,
it was unlikely his request would be granted.
Yuè insisted on arguing for it,
and Hao was indeed vindicated,
which was praised in public opinion.
Later he became the Left Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel."
Jiǎnwén said,
"Why is it that you have gone white first?"
He replied:
"The appearance of a willow tree
withers at the sight of autumn;
the nature of pine and cypress
thrives even more after experiencing frost."
Gù Kǎi zhī's biography of his father states:
"You, sir, declined in the world because of your uprightness.
When you entered the king's presence,
the king did not have a single grey hair,
but you, sir, were already grey-haired.
When the king asked your age,
you then said:
'Why are you so prematurely white-haired?'
You replied:
'The appearance of pine and cypress
still thrives after experiencing frost;
I am of the nature of a willow tree,
withering before autumn arrives.
It is a difference in fate.'
The king praised his words for a long time."
Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) entered the gorge,
with sheer cliffs suspended in the sky,
and turbulent waves rushing swiftly.
The *Jìn Yáng Qiū* says:
"Wēn, in the second year of the Yǒnghé era
led more than seven thousand men to attack Shǔ,
presented his memorial and immediately departed."
Thereupon, he sighed and said:
"Having become a loyal minister,
I cannot be a filial son,
what to do?"
The *Book of Han* says:
"Wáng Yáng was appointed Inspector of Yìzhōu.
When he made an inspection tour and arrived at the Nine-Bend Slope of Qióngbó,
he sighed and said:
'I bear the remains of my ancestors.
How can I repeatedly ride on this dangerous path!'
He resigned from office due to illness.
Later, Wáng Zūn was appointed Inspector.
When he arrived at the slope,
he asked the official,
'Is this the road that Wáng Yáng feared?'
The official said:
'It is!'
He scolded his driver, saying:
'Drive on!
Wáng Yáng was a filial son,
Wáng Zūn is a loyal minister.'"
Initially,
Mars entered Tàiwēi,
and soon after, Hǎixī was deposed.
The *Annals of Jìn* says:
"In the intercalary tenth month of the sixth year of the Tài Hé era,
Mars guarded the Duānmén (End Gate) of Tàiwēi.
In the eleventh month,
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn deposed the emperor and made him the Duke of Hǎixī.
The "Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn" states:
"Huán Wēn suffered a devastating defeat at Fāngtóu.
Knowing that he had lost the people's support,
he then massacred Yuán Zhēn in Shòuyáng.
Afterwards, he said to Xī Chāo:
'Is this enough to wipe away the shame of Fāngtóu?'
Chāo said:
'It is not enough to satisfy the sentiments of those who understand.
At the age of sixty,
you were defeated in a major campaign.
If you do not establish a great and lasting achievement,
it will not be enough to suppress and satisfy the people's expectations.'
He then persuaded Wēn about the matter of deposing and establishing a new emperor.
At the time, Wēn had long harbored this intention,
and he deeply accepted Chāo's words,
and so he deposed the Duke of Hǎixī."
Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
and Mars again entered the Tàiwēi asterism,
which the Emperor detested.
Xú Guǎng's "Annals of Jìn" states:
"In the twelfth month of the first year of Xián'ān (371),
Mars retrograded and entered the Tàiwēi asterism,
and by the seventh month of the second year (372),
it was still there.
The Emperor, mindful of the Hǎixī affair,
was greatly worried about this.
At that time, Xī Chāo was a Zhongshū (Secretary) on duty.
The *Zhongxing Shu* says:
"Chāo's style name was Jǐngxīng.
He was a native of Gāopíng,
and the son of Sīkōng Yīn.
In his youth, he was outstanding and unrestrained,
possessing a breadth of vision rarely seen in the world.
He was successively promoted to Zhongshū Láng (Secretary),
and Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works)."
The Emperor called Chāo in and said:
"Whether Heaven decrees a long or short life
is not something to be concerned about.
I only ask that there be no recurrence of recent events."
Chāo said:
"The Grand General is about to secure the borders externally
and stabilize the country internally.
He will certainly not have such thoughts.
Your subject will vouch for him with a hundred lives."
The Emperor then recited Yǔ Zhòngchū's poem (Yǔ Chǎn's *Cong Zheng Shi*).
He said:
"Patriots grieve for the perilous state of the court;
loyal ministers lament the humiliation of their lord."
His voice was exceedingly mournful.
Xī accepted leave and returned east.
The Emperor said:
"Convey my regards to your esteemed father.
The affairs of the family and the state
have come to this!
Therefore, I was unable to use the Dao to correct and protect [the state],
and to think ahead and prevent disasters.
The depth of my shame and regret
cannot be expressed in words."
Thereupon, he wept, and tears flowed down his front.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* (Continuation of the *Spring and Autumn Annals of Jìn*) says:
"The Emperor outwardly suppressed powerful ministers,
worried and resentful, and did not achieve his ambitions.
He collapsed after being on the throne for two years."
Emperor Jiǎnwén sat in a dark room,
and summoned Xuānwǔ.
Xuānwǔ arrived,
and asked where the Emperor was.
Jiǎnwén said:
"I am here."
People at the time thought this was skillful.
The *Lúnyǔ* (Analects) says:
"When the Music Master Miǎn came to visit,
and reached the steps,
the Master said:
'These are the steps.'
When he reached the mat,
the Master said:
'This is the mat.'
When everyone was seated,
the Master told him:
'So-and-so is here,
Someone is here.'"
Commentary:
"It means he told everyone seated there."
Jiǎn Wén entered Huá Lín Garden,
and turning to those around him, said:
"A place to meet the heart,
need not be far away.
The shady forest and waters,
naturally bring about the Háo
and Pú idle thoughts.
Háo and Pú,
are names of two rivers.
《Zhuāngzǐ》says:
"Zhuāngzǐ was strolling with Huìzǐ on the Háo Liáng Bridge,
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'The minnows come out and swim freely,
this is the joy of the fish.'
Huìzǐ said:
'You are not a fish,
how do you know the joy of the fish?'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'You are not me,
how do you know that I do not know the joy of the fish?'"
"Zhuāng Zhōu was fishing on the Pú River,
The King of Chǔ sent two grand officers to visit him,
saying:
'I wish to trouble Zhuāngzǐ with affairs of my territory.'
Zhuāngzǐ held his fishing rod without looking back,
and said:
"I have heard that in Chǔ there was a divine turtle
that died three thousand years ago,
wrapped in cloth and stored in a chest in the temple.
Would it rather drag its tail in the mud,
or have its bones preserved and be valued?"
The two high officials said:
"It would rather drag its tail in the mud."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Go away!
I too would rather drag my tail in the mud."
He awakened the birds and beasts, fowl and fish,
and they came of their own accord to be close to people."
Xiè Tàifù spoke to Wáng Yòujūn, saying:
"In middle age, I am wounded by sorrow and joy,
and when I part with relatives and friends,
I invariably feel bad for several days."
Wáng said:
The "Wénzì Zhì" states:
"Wáng Xīzhī's courtesy name was Yìshǎo,
from Lángyá, Línyí.
His father was Kuàng,
the Governor of Huáinán.
Xīzhī was intelligent and outstanding from a young age,
and was appreciated by his uncle Yí.
He excelled at cursive and clerical script,
He was successively promoted to the positions of Prefect of Jiāngzhōu 江州,
General of the Right Army,
and Intendant of Kuàijī 會稽."
"Being of advanced age,
I have naturally reached this point.
I rely solely on music to find solace.
I am constantly afraid that my children will notice
and spoil the joy of it."
Zhī Dàolín 支道林 often kept several horses.
Someone said that it was unseemly for a Daoist to keep horses.
Zhī 支 said:
"This poor Daoist values their spirit and swiftness."
*Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:
"Zhī Dùn 支遁, courtesy name Dàolín 道林,
was from Línlǜ 林慮, Hénèi 河內;
some say he was from Chénliú 陳留;
his original surname was Guān 關.
From a young age, he was self-willed and independent,
with a noble and bright demeanor.
His family had long been devoted to Buddhism.
He once meditated on the principles of the Way in the mountains of Yúháng 餘杭,
feeling detached and alone.
At the age of twenty-five, he renounced worldly form and entered the Way.
He passed away in Luòyáng 洛陽 at the age of fifty-three."
Liú Yǐn 劉尹 and Huán Xuānwǔ 桓宣武 were together listening to a lecture on the *Book of Rites*.
Huán 桓 said:
"When there is a place that enters the heart,
one then perceives the mysterious gate to be within a short distance."
Liú said:
"This does not relate to the ultimate,
it is merely the language of the Golden Flower Hall."
The "Narrative Biography of the History of the Han" says:
"Bān Bó received the 《Book of Poetry》 from Shī Dān when he was young.
The General-in-Chief Wáng Fèng recommended Bó to Emperor Chéng,
suggesting he should encourage learning.
The Emperor summoned him for intimate banquets,
and appointed him as a Palace Attendant.
At that time, the Emperor was inclined towards learning,
and Zhèng Kuānzhōng,
and Zhāng Yǔ would enter the Golden Flower Hall morning and evening to explain the 《Book of Documents》
and the 《Analects》,
and the Emperor ordered Bó to receive instruction from them."
Yáng Bǐng served as a military advisor to the Pacification Army,
and died young,
enjoying a reputation for excellence.
Yōu Hóu Xiàorùo wrote a preface for him,
expressing extreme praise and lament.
《Preface to Yáng Bǐng》 says:
"Bǐng's courtesy name was Chángdá,
he was from Píngyáng in Tàishān.
He was the great-great-grandson of the Governor of Nányáng during the Hàn Dynasty.
His grandfather was the Prefect of Wèijùn,
namely Yuán Zǐ, the clerk of the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
The Prefect's wife, Zhèng Shì 鄭氏, had no son,
so she adopted Bǐng 秉.
When he was young, he was excellent,
being careful, respectful, and cautious.
At the age of ten, Lady Zhèng 鄭 died,
and Bǐng 秉 exhausted his grief in remembering her countenance.
Soon after, the Prefect's clerk and the Lady both passed away.
Bǐng's 秉 cousins and paternal relatives
followed the proper rites,
and people could not distinguish them from his own parents,
so harmonious were they.
He served as a consultant in the affairs of the抚军將軍 (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, General Who Pacifies the Army),
ready to unleash his potential for great achievements,
and to soar with wings reaching for the heavens.
Alas, he died at the age of thirty-two.
In the past, when Hǎn Hǔ 罕虎 died,
Zǐchǎn 子產 lamented that there was no one left to do good with.
Since the death of Fūzǐ 夫子 (Confucius),
there has been a similar lament as that of Zǐchǎn 子產!
After his death, his son died young as well.
Why is it that doing good deeds results in such great misfortune?
Could it be the bewilderment of Sīmǎ Shēng 司馬生?"
Yáng Quán 羊權 served as a Gentleman Attendant in the Yellow Gate.
He attended Emperor Jiǎnwén 簡文.
The Emperor asked,
"Xiàhóu Zhàn's 夏侯湛 separate views
in writing the "Preface to Yáng Bǐng 羊秉" are absolutely delightful.
What sort of person are you?
"Does he have descendants?"
The *Yáng Shì Pǔ* (Genealogy of the Yáng Clan) says:
"Quán, zi Dàoyú,
was the son of Xú Zhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xu Province) Chén.
He served and rose to the position of Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs)."
Quán, with tears welling up, replied:
"My deceased uncle Lìngwèn's early reputation was well-known,
but he had no successors.
Although his name spread throughout the empire,
his lineage has been cut off in this enlightened era."
The Emperor sighed with emotion for a long time.
Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) Wáng and Zhēncháng (Honorary Title) Liú met again after parting.
The *Wáng Chángshǐ Bié Zhuàn* (Separate Biography of Chief Clerk Wáng) says:
"Méng, zi Zhòngzǔ,
was a native of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His ancestors came from the Zhōu royal house.
Through the Hàn and
Wèi dynasties, they were a prominent family for generations.
His grandfather was Zuǒ,
Běijūn Zhōnghòu (Commander of the Northern Army).
His father was Nè,
Yè Lìng (Magistrate of Ye).
Méng's spirit and demeanor were clear and beautiful.
At the age of ten,
he was unrestrained and stood out from the crowd.
At the age of twenty, his deportment was esteemed.
His bearing was elegant and upright.
He outwardly rejected glory and competition,
and inwardly reduced selfish desires.
He was summoned (bì) as an assistant (yuàn) by the Minister of Education (Sītú),
and as a secretary (láng) in the Palace Library (Zhōngshū).
Because he was the stepfather of the Empress, he was posthumously awarded the title of Grand Master of Palace Light (Guānglù Dàfū)."
Wáng said to Liú:
"You are further progressing."
He replied:
"This is like the sky being high of itself."
The "Yǔ Lín" (Forest of Discourse) says:
"Zhòngzǔ spoke to Zhēncháng, saying:
'You have recently made great progress.'
Liú said:
'Are you looking up?'
Wáng asked what he meant.
Liú said:
'If not,
how could you measure the height of the sky?'"
Liú Yǐn said:
"People imagine Wáng Jīngchǎn to be excellent;
this is like imagining there must be a pure breeze under a tall pine."
Jīngchǎn was
Wáng Huī's childhood name.
The "Wáng Family Genealogy" says:
"Huī's courtesy name was Yòurén,
a native of Lángyá.
His grandfather was Yì,
Píngběi Jiāngjūn (平北將軍),

Wáng Zhòngzǔ (王仲祖) heard the barbarian language and did not understand it,

The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* (春秋傳) says:

He was asked about it, and it proved to be true."
Dù Yù's (杜預) commentary says:

Liú Zhēncháng (劉真長) was the Yin (尹) of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Xǔ Xuándù (許玄度) left the capital to stay with Liú (劉).

He was the great-great-grandson of Wèi Zhōnglǐngjūn Yǔn.

When he grew up, his temperament was simple and unadorned.
The Sītú summoned him as an official,

Beds and curtains were newly luxurious,

Xǔ said:

Liú said:

Wáng Yìshǎo, who was present, said:

Wáng Yòujūn and Xiè Tàifù together climbed Yěchéng.

"Yěchéng,
was where coins were cast in the time of Wú.
Wú Píng,

Xiè, lost in distant thought,

Now the four borders are surrounded by ramparts,

Everyone should offer their services.

The *Zhànguó Cè* says:

Could it be that pure speech invites trouble?"
Grand Tutor Xiè gathered his family on a cold snowy day,

Suddenly, the snow fell heavily,

"What does the white snow falling profusely resemble?"
His nephew, Hú’ér, said:

"It's somewhat like scattering salt in the air."

Gōng laughed heartily with joy.
This was Gōng's elder brother, Wú Yì's daughter,

Záochǐ believed that Shénnóng was born in Qiánzhōng,
the "Shaonan" poems praised his beautiful transformation,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* said he had many talents,
the style of "Han Guang"

Zǐ Wén and
Shū Áo
were ashamed to compare their virtues with Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Zǐ.
The song of Jiē Yú, "Phoenix, oh phoenix,"
and the fisherman's chant, "The Canglang River,"
The old man of Han Yin rebuked Zǐ Gòng,
Yí Liáo of South Market and
Tu Yángyuè did not turn back for the sake of profit,
Lǔ Zhònglián is not as good as the old couple Lǎo Lái;

Dèng Yǔ,

Comparing their people,

examining their customs,

tracing their history,
there were no rebels like the Red Eyebrows or Yellow Turbans.
How does this compare to Qīngzhōu?"
Tāo debated back and forth with him,
and Záo Chǐ had nothing to say in response.
Upon completion,
he showed it to Hán Kāngbó.
Kāngbó remained silent,
and the king said,
"Why do you not speak?"
Hán said,
"There is nothing to approve or disapprove."
Mǎ Róng, in his commentary on the *Analects*, said,
"Only where righteousness lies."
Liú Yǐn said:
"Whenever there is a clear breeze and bright moon,
I invariably think of Xuán Dù."
*Jìn Zhōngxīng Shìrén Shū* says:
"Xǔ Xún was capable of pure conversation,

When Xún Zhōngláng was in Jīngkǒu,

"Xún Xiàn, styled Lìngzé,

frequently visiting Yìxīng and
Wú Commandery.
He was promoted beyond rank to General of the North Central Army and
Governor of Xú Province,

*Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Xiàn, at the age of twenty-eight,
He was appointed to govern the two provinces of Xú (徐) and
Yǎn (兗).

like Xiàn (羡)."
He climbed Běigù (北固) and looked out at the sea, saying:

"Northwest of the city, there is a separate ridge that enters the river,
surrounded by water on three sides,
several tens of *zhàng* in height,

"Although I have not yet seen the three immortal mountains,

Hàn (漢) dynasties were here,

The *Shǐjì Fēngshàn Shū* (史記封禪書, Book of Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the *Records of the Grand Historian*) says:
"Pénglái (蓬萊),
Fāngzhàng (方丈), and
Yíngzhōu (瀛洲) are these three immortal mountains,
legend has it they are in the sea,
not far from people.
There have been those who reached them,

The palaces are made of gold and silver,

looking like clouds from afar.
But upon arrival,
they are actually located underwater.
Wanting to arrive,
the wind would immediately draw the boat away,
and in the end, no one could reach it.
Qín Shǐhuáng climbed Mount Kuàijī,
and traveled along the seacoast,
hoping to find the wondrous medicine of the Three Divine Mountains.
Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty, after performing the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
without wind or rain bringing any change,
the alchemists further said that the various medicines of Pénglái could be obtained,
thereupon the emperor happily went east to the sea,
hoping to obtain those from Pénglái."
Lord Xiè said:
"The distance between the virtuous and sages and ordinary people
is also close."
His nephews and nieces did not agree with this.
Lord Xiè sighed and said:
"If Xī Chāo heard these words,
he certainly would not consider them as far away as the Milky Way."
The *Biography of Chāo* says:
"Chāo was skilled in principles and meanings,
The śramaṇa Zhī Dàolín considered him a leading talent of his time."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Jiānwú asked Liánshū, saying:
'I heard words from Jiēyú,
grand yet without substance,
going forth and not returning.
I find his words strange and frightening,
"It is like the Milky Way, without end."
Zhī Gōng 支公 loved cranes.
He lived on the Dōngyǎng East Mountain in Shàn 剡.
The *Zhī Gōng Shū* 支公書 says:
"The mountain is two hundred *lǐ* 里 from Huìjī 會稽."
Someone gifted him a pair of cranes.
In a short time, their wings grew long and they were about to fly.
Zhī 支, feeling pity for them,
clipped their wing feathers.
The cranes tried to soar but were no longer able to fly.
They then looked back at their wings,
lowered their heads to look at them,
as if with a sense of regret.
Lín 林 said:
"Since they have the bearing to reach the clouds,
how could they be willing to be made into mere playthings for people's eyes and ears?"
He kept them until their feathers grew back,
and then let them fly away.
Xiè Zhōngláng 謝中郎 passed by Qū'ā 曲阿 Later Lake.
He asked his attendants:
"What water is this?"
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* 中興書 says:
"Xiè Wàn 謝萬, courtesy name Wànshí 萬石,
was the younger brother of Grand Tutor Ān 安.
He possessed high talent and spirit,
and gained fame early on.
(He) successively held the positions of Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
General of the Western Central Army,
Governor of Yuzhou,
and Attendant Gentleman at the Palace Gate."
(He) replied:
"Lake Qu'a."
"The Great Kang Topography" says:
"Qu'a was originally named Yunyang.
The First Emperor of Qin, believing it possessed royal aura,
carved into Mount Beikeng to break its power,
cut off its straight road,
making its 'a' curved,

The Wu Dynasty restored it to Yunyang,
now it is again named Qu'a."
Xiè (Ān) said:
"It should be like a deep pool accumulating and settling,

Emperor Wu of Jin always gave Shān Tāo meager gifts.
(This) was Xiè Tàifù Ān.
(He) asked his nephews and sons,
(namely) Chēqí (General of Chariots and Cavalry) Xuán.
(He) replied:
"It must be because those who desire (the gifts) are few,

"The Family Biography of Xiè, the General of Chariots and Cavalry" says:
"Xuán's courtesy name was Yòudù,
Zhèn Xī 奕's third son.
Spiritually intelligent and bright,
good at subtle language.
His uncle, Grand Tutor, once held a gathering with his nephews and nieces.

and asked,
"Hú wéi hū ní zhōng?"
It is the "Shì Wēi" poem of Wèi.
Máo Gōng said:
"Ní zhōng,
is the name of a city of Wèi." The answer says:
"Bó yán wǎng sù,
féng bǐ zhī nù."
It is the "Bǎi Zhōu" poem of Wèi and Bèi.
Fú Qián was well-versed in the *Chūn Qiū*,
and was about to write a commentary on it.
He wanted to consult on the similarities and differences.
He heard that Cuī Liè was gathering his disciples to lecture and transmit knowledge.
Zhì Yú's *Wén Zhāng Zhì* says:
"Liè's zi is Wēi Kǎo.
He was from Ān Píng in Gāoyáng,
the grandson of Yīn,
and the nephew of Yuàn.
During the time of Emperor Líng,
he held official positions such as Sītú
and Tàiwèi,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángpíng."
So he hid his name
and worked as a hired cook for Liè's disciples.
Whenever it was time for a lecture,
he would secretly listen from between the door and wall.
Once he knew that (Cuī Liè) couldn't surpass him,
he gradually began to discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the various students.
Liè heard this,
I cannot fathom who he is,
but I have long heard of Qián's reputation,
and I suspected it was him.
The next morning, I went to see him.
Before he was awake,
I called out,
"Zǐ Shèn! Zǐ Shèn!"
Qián unconsciously responded in surprise,
and they became friends.
Zhōng Huì composed the "Treatise on the Four Fundamentals." Once it was completed,
he greatly desired to have Jī Gōng read it once.
He placed it in his bosom,
and once he had decided to do it,
he feared his difficulty,
and dared not take it out,
but threw it remotely from outside the door,
and then quickly ran away.
The "History of Wei" says:
"Huì discussed the similarities and differences in talent and nature,
which was passed down to the world.
The 'Four Fundamentals' are:
saying that talent and nature are the same,
talent and nature are different,
talent and nature are united,
and talent and nature are separated.
The Gentleman of the Secretariat Fù Gǔ argued for sameness,
the Imperial Secretary Lǐ Fēng argued for difference,
the Palace Attendant Zhōng Huì argued for union,
and the Commandant of the Cavalry Wáng Guǎng argued for separation.
Much of the text is not recorded."
Hé Yàn served as Minister of Personnel,
and had position and prestige.
At that time, his seat was filled with discussion guests.
The "Wénzhāng Xùlù" states:
"Yàn was skilled at pure conversation,
and being powerful at the time,
all the debaters in the empire
mostly revered and followed him."
The "Wèi Shì Chūnqiū" states:
"Yàn possessed unusual talent from a young age,
and was good at discussing the *Yì* and *Lǎo* (Book of Changes and Laozi)."
Wáng Bì visited him before reaching adulthood.
Yàn had heard of Bì's name.
The "Bì Bié Zhuàn" states:
"Bì's courtesy name was Fǔsì,
he was from Gāopíng in Shānyáng.
He was perceptive and intelligent from a young age,
and liked *Zhuāng* and *Lǎo* (Zhuangzi and Laozi) from his teens.
He was eloquent and skilled in debate,
and was recognized by Fù Gǔ.
The Líbù Shàngshū Hé Yàn greatly admired him,
and inscribed of him:
'The younger generation is to be feared.
A person like this
can discuss the boundary between Heaven and humanity!'
He appointed Bì as a Táiláng (Palace Attendant).
Bì's strong suit was certainly not practical matters,
so he paid even less attention to them,
and often laughed at people for their strengths,
therefore he was envied by the scholars of the time."
Moreover, he was shallow and did not understand human nature.
Initially, he was on good terms with Wáng Lí and Xún Róng,
but Wáng Lí took his position as Gentleman Attendant,
and so he resented Wáng Lí.
His relationship with Xún Róng also did not remain good to the end.
During the Zhèngshǐ period, he was dismissed from office due to official business.
That autumn, he died of a severe illness,
at the age of twenty-four.
When [Hé Yán] died,
Emperor Jǐng of the Jìn Dynasty sighed with regret for several days,
and said,
"Heaven has taken him from me!"
Such was the extent to which those with profound understanding mourned and regretted him."
He then listed the superior principles he had previously discussed and said to [Hé Yán]:
"I think this principle is the ultimate;
can it be refuted again?"
[Hé Yán] then raised objections,
and everyone present immediately thought he was defeated.
Thereupon, [Hé Yán] acted as both guest and host several times,
and none of those present could match him.
When Hé Píngshū finished annotating the *Lǎozǐ*,
He visited Wáng Fǔsì 王輔嗣.
Seeing that Wáng's 王 commentary was remarkably insightful and extraordinary,
he was deeply impressed and said,
"Such a man
is worthy of discussing the boundary between Heaven and humanity!"
He then used his commentary to create the "Two Treatises on Dào Dé".
The *Wèi Shì Chūn Qiū* 魏氏春秋 says:
"Bì's 弼 exposition of the Dào is less concise and beautiful than that of Yàn 晏,
but his natural talent and brilliance surpass him."
When Wáng Fǔsì 王輔嗣, barely of age, visited Péi Huī 裴徽,
the *Yǒng Jiā Liúrén Míng* 永嘉流人名 says:
"Huī 徽, courtesy name Wénjì 文季,
was from Wénxǐ 聞喜, Hédōng 河東.
He was the younger brother of the Grand Master of Ceremonies, Qián 潛.
He rose to the position of Inspector of Jìzhōu 冀州."
Huī 徽 asked,
"The Non-Being
is truly that on which all things rely.
Sages are reluctant to speak about it,
yet Lǎozǐ 老子 endlessly emphasizes it. Why is that?"
The *Bì Bié Zhuàn* 弼別傳 says:
"Bì's 弼 father was a Gentleman of the Secretariat,
and Péi Huī 裴徽 was a Gentleman of the Bureau of Appointments.
Huī 徽 saw his exceptional talent
and therefore asked."
Bì 弼 replied,
"Sages embody Non-Being,
but Non-Being cannot be instructed.
Therefore, their speech invariably involves "being" (有);
even Lǎo and Zhuāng cannot escape "being,"
and constantly instruct about what is lacking."
Fù Gǔ was skilled at speaking about the victory of emptiness (虛勝).
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
"[Fù] Gǔ, courtesy name Lánshuò,
was a native of Nìyáng in Běidì,
a descendant of Fù Jièzi.
He successively rose to the positions of Governor of Hénán,
and Palace Secretary.
[Fù] Gǔ once discussed *Talent and Nature, Similarities and Differences*;
Zhōng Huì gathered people to discuss it."
The *Fù Zǐ* states:
"[Fù] Gǔ was both versed in governance and fond of rectitude,
and he possessed discerning wisdom that grasped the essentials.
For example, in his discourse on talent and nature,
he traced back to the fundamental subtleties,
which few could match.
Zhōng Huì, the Director of Retainers (司隸) was very young,
[Fù] Gǔ associated with him based on his intelligence."
Xún Càn's discussions favored the profound and distant. The *Càn Biézhuàn* states:
"[Xún] Càn, courtesy name Fèngqiàn,
was a native of Yǐnyīn in Yǐngchuān,
the youngest son of Grand Commandant Yù.
[Xún] Càn's elder brothers were each known for their Confucian scholarship and debates.
[Xún] Càn was skilled in speaking of the profound and distant,
and often cited Zǐgòng's saying:
'The Master's discourse on nature (性) and the Way of Heaven (天道)
It cannot be heard.'
In that case, though the Six Classics survive,
they are merely the chaff and dross of the sages.
Those who are good at speaking cannot prevail."
Whenever they spoke together,
there were disputes and they could not understand each other.
Péi Jìzhōu (裴冀州) explained the meanings of the two schools,
understanding the feelings of both sides,
and always enabled both parties to gain something,
and both sides were delighted.
The *Biography of Càn* says:
"When Càn (粲) first arrived in the capital during the Tài Hé (太和) period,
he discussed with Fù Gǔ (傅嘏), who was skilled in names and principles,
but Càn (粲) valued the abstruse and distant.
Although their underlying principles were the same,
in moments of haste they sometimes clashed
and were unable to appreciate each other's point of view.
Péi Huī (裴徽) understood the feelings of both sides
and explained them for the two schools.
Soon after, Càn (粲) and Gǔ (嘏) became friendly."
The *Biography of Guǎn Lù* says:
"Administrator Péi (裴) had great talent and unrestrained manner,
and was good at discussing the profound and subtle."
Hé Yàn (何晏) had not finished his commentary on the *Laozi*,
when he saw Wáng Bì (王弼) explaining the meaning of his own commentary on the *Laozi*.
Hé (何) felt that his own ideas had many shortcomings,
and could no longer make a sound,
but only responded with "yes, yes."
Thereupon, he did not write any more commentaries,
and subsequently composed the "Essay on the Dao and De".
The "Preface to Literary Works" states:
"Since Confucian scholars argued that Laozi was not a sage,
rejecting ritual and abandoning learning,
Yàn's explanation was the same as that of the sages,
and his essay circulated in the world."
During the Central Dynasty,
there were followers who cherished the Dao,
and some went to Wáng Yífǔ to consult him about their doubts.
It happened that Wáng had already spoken much the day before,
and was a little tired,
so he could not respond,
and said to the guest:
"I am feeling a little unwell now,
Péi Yìmín is also nearby,
you can go and ask him."
The "Eulogies of the Dukes of Jin" states:
"Péi Wèi's discourse on principles
was not inferior to that of Wáng Yífǔ."
Péi Chénggōng wrote the "Essay on Honoring Being,"
and people of the time attacked and challenged it,
but no one could refute it.
Only Wáng Yífǔ came,
and he seemed to be slightly humbled.
People then used Wáng's principles to challenge Péi,
and the principles were further elaborated.
The "Eulogies of the Dukes of Jin" states:
"From Wèi Tài Cháng Xiàhóu Xuán
, and Bùbīng Xiàowèi Ruǎn Jí,
all wrote "Discussions on the Dao and Virtue" (Dàodé Lùn).
At that time, Shìzhōng Yuè Guǎng,
and Lìbù Láng Liú Hàn also embodied the Dao and spoke concisely.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yífǔ
discussed principles but lacked substance.
Sànqí Chángshì Dài Ào made studying the Dao his profession.
Later, Yǔ Kǎi and others all admired simplicity and broadness.
Wěi disliked the common custom of valuing the principles of emptiness and nothingness,
therefore, he wrote two essays, "Elevating Existence" (Chóng Yǒu), to refute them.
His talent was broad, and his analogies were extensive,
so scholars could not exhaustively understand them.
Later, Yuè Guǎng wanted to discuss principles with Wěi in a relaxed setting,
but Wěi's explanations were abundant and comprehensive.
Guǎng, considering himself to embody emptiness and nothingness,
smiled and said nothing more."
"The Record of Activity of Emperor Huì" (Huì Dì Qǐjūzhù) says:
"Wěi wrote two essays to correct the flaws of emptiness and extravagance.
His writing was refined and rich,
making them famous essays of the time."
Zhūgě Gōng was unwilling to study when he was young.
He began talking with Wáng Yífǔ,
and immediately reached a profound level.
Wáng sighed and said:
"Your talent is outstanding,
if you would add a little research,
yī wú suǒ kuì." "Nothing to be ashamed of."
Hóng hòu kàn "Zhuāng," "Lǎo,"
gèng yǔ Wáng yǔ,
biàn zú xiāng kànghéng. Hóng later read "Zhuangzi" and "Laozi," and further spoke with Wáng, and was thus sufficient to contend with him.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" rì:
"Hóng zì Màoyuǎn,
Lángyá rén,
Wèi Yōngzhōu cìshǐ Xù zhī zǐ.
Yǒu yì cái,

shì zhì Sīkōng zhǔbù." Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jin" says: "Hóng's courtesy name was Màoyuǎn, he was from Lángyá, and the son of Xù, the Inspector of Yōng Province during the Wei dynasty. He had extraordinary talent and served as a Principal Clerk in the Ministry of Works."
Wèi Jiè zǒngjiǎo shí wèn Yuè Lìng "mèng,"
Yuè yún "shì xiǎng." When Wèi Jiè was still a youth, he asked Yuè Lìng about "dreams," and Yuè said, "It is thought."
Wèi yuē:
"xíng shén suǒ bù jiē ér mèng,
qǐ shì xiǎng xié?" Wèi said, "The body and spirit do not connect during a dream, how can it be thought?"
Yuè yún:
"yīn yě.
Wèi cháng mèng chéng chē rù shǔ xué,
dǎo jī dàn tiě chǔ,

jiē wú xiǎng wú yīn gù yě." Yuè said: "It is cause. You have never dreamed of riding a carriage into a rat hole or pounding pickles to eat with an iron pestle, all because there is no thought and no cause."
"Zhōu Lǐ" yǒu liù mèng:
yī yuē zhèng mèng,
wèi wú suǒ gǎndòng,
píng'ān ér mèng yě. The "Rites of Zhou" has six kinds of dreams: first is the correct dream, meaning dreaming in peace without any stimulation.
èr yuē è mèng,
wèi jīng'è ér mèng yě. Second is the nightmare, meaning dreaming in fright.
sān yuē sī mèng,
This refers to what is thought about when awake.
Fourth is *wù mèng*,
referring to dreaming while awake and speaking about it.
Fifth is *xǐ mèng*,
referring to dreaming due to joyful narration.
Sixth is *jù mèng*,
referring to dreaming due to fear.
According to what Yuè said,
"thinking"
refers to *sī mèng*.
"Cause"
refers to *zhèng mèng*.
Wèi was thinking about the "cause",
could not understand it for days,
and subsequently fell ill.
Yuè heard about it,
so he ordered his carriage to be prepared to analyze it for him.
Wèi recovered a little.
Yuè sighed and said:
"This child must have no illness in his heart that would reach the vital regions!"
The *Chūn Qiū Zhuàn* says:
"Duke Jǐng of Jìn had an illness
and sought a doctor from Qín.
The Duke of Qín sent the doctor Huǎn to treat him.
Before he arrived,
the Duke dreamed that the illness was two small children.
They said:
'He is a good doctor.
I fear it will harm me!'
One of them said:
'It dwells above the huāng,
below the gāo,
what can be done to me?'
The doctor arrived and said:
'The illness is beyond cure!
It is above the huāng,
below the gāo,
attacking it cannot reach,
stabbing it cannot touch,
medicine cannot reach it.'
The Duke said:
'A truly excellent doctor.'」
Commentary:
'Huāng,
is the diaphragm.
Below the heart is gāo.'」
Yǔ Zǐsōng read "Zhuangzi",
he opened the scroll about a foot and then put it down,
and said:
'It does not differ from what people think.'
The "Spring and Autumn Annals of Jin" says:
'Yǔ Kǎi, courtesy name Zǐsōng,
was from Yǐngchuān,
the third son of the Palace Attendant Jùn.
He was generous and had great capacity,
he considered himself a follower of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
He said:
"Formerly, before reading this book,
I often thought that ultimate truth was like this.
Now that I see it,
it exactly matches what people intuitively think."
He rose to the position of Prefect of Yùzhōu.
When a guest asked Lè Lìng about the meaning of "Zhǐ bù zhì" (the concept of "meaning not arriving"),
Lè also didn't break down and analyze the sentences,
but directly tapped the table with the handle of his horsetail whisk and said:
"Does it arrive?"
The guest said: "It arrives!"
Lè then raised the horsetail whisk again and said:
"If it arrives, how can it leave?"
Now, consider a hidden boat sailing,
people crossing arms constantly excuse one another.
Not a single breath lingers,
suddenly appearing and disappearing.
Therefore, the shadow of a flying bird,
no one sees it move;
the wheels of a speeding carriage,
never seem to touch the ground.
Thus, going and not going,
how can there be arriving?
Arriving and not arriving,
how can there be going?
However, arriving before is no different from arriving later,
the name "arriving" is thus produced;
Going before is no different from going after;
going is how names are established.
Today, under Heaven, there is no going;
how can going be anything but false?
Since it is already false,
how can coming be real?
Thereupon the guest finally understood and submitted.
The *Yue* texts are concise, yet their meanings are clear;
they are all of this kind.
Initially, there were dozens of commentators on the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
none of whom could fully grasp its essential meaning.
Xiàng Xiù, in addition to the old commentaries, provided explanations,
subtly analyzing its unique essence,
greatly opening up the mysterious style.
The *Xiù Bié Zhuàn* says:
"Xiù was friends with Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān,
but their preferences differed.
Jī Kāng was proud and unrestrained,
Ān was free-spirited and transcended convention,
while Xiù was refined and loved to read.
The two often mocked him for this.
Later, when Xiù was about to comment on the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
he first told Kāng and Ān.
Kāng and Ān both said:
'Does this book still need commentary?
It's just giving up people's enjoyable pursuits!'
When it was completed,
he showed it to the two men.
Kāng said,
"Will you still be victorious?"
Ān then exclaimed in surprise,
"Zhuāng Zhōu is not dead!"
Later, he annotated the *Book of Changes* (*Zhōu Yì*),
the general meaning of which was worth observing,
but he had differences with the various Confucian scholars of the Hàn Dynasty,
not being as outstanding as Yǐn and Zhuāng."
The main biography of Xiù perhaps says,
that Xiù relied on several worthy men in his travels,
and spent his years idly,
without any commentaries.
He only loved the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
and casually responded to what Cuī Zhuàn had annotated,
in order to prevent forgetting, it is said.
The *Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* (*Zhúlín Qīxián Lùn*) says,
"Xiù wrote this meaning,
and whoever reads it cannot help but feel transcendent,
as if they have already left the dust and are peering into the utter darkness,
and have begun to understand what lies beyond sight and sound.
He possessed divine virtue and profound wisdom,
capable of abandoning the world,
and externalizing all things.
Even if those who are driven by competition turn to look at what they pursue,
they will all be filled with a sense of disappointment and a desire to free themselves."
Only the two chapters "Autumn Floods" (*Qiū Shuǐ*) and "Supreme Happiness" (*Zhì Lè*) were unfinished when Xiù died.
Xiù's son was young,
and the meaning was scattered and lost,
However, there was still another version.
Guō Xiàng 郭象,
was a man of shallow conduct
but possessed outstanding talent.
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* 文士傳 states:
"Xiàng 象, styled Zǐxuán 子玄,
was a native of Hénán 河南.
He was intelligent and rational from a young age,
admired the Dào 道 and loved learning,
relying on Lǎo 老 and Zhuāng 莊.
People at the time generally considered him to be second only to Wáng Bì 王弼.
He was summoned as a clerk by the Minister of Works and
as a secretary by the Grand Tutor."
Seeing that Xiàng Xiù's 向秀 interpretation was not being transmitted to the world,
he then secretly treated it as if he had annotated it himself.
He then personally annotated the "Qiū Shuǐ 秋水" (Autumn Floods) and "Zhì Lè 至樂" (Perfect Happiness) two chapters,
and also changed the "Mǎ Tí 馬蹄" (Horses' Hooves) chapter,
while for the rest of the chapters,
he only corrected punctuation and phrasing.
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* 文士傳 states:
"Xiàng 象's *Zhuāngzǐ Zhù* 莊子注 (Commentary on the *Zhuāngzǐ* )
possesses the most elegant phrasing and profound meaning."
Later, Xiàng Xiù's 向秀 original version came out,
therefore today there exist two *Zhuāngzǐ* 莊子 texts, those of Xiàng 向 and Guō 郭,
whose meanings are the same.
Ruǎn Xuānzǐ 阮宣子 had a good reputation.
Grand Commandant Wáng Yífǔ 王夷甫 saw him and asked:
"Are Lǎo 老 and Zhuāng 莊 the same or different from the teachings of the sages?"
He replied:
"Will there be no agreement?"
The Grand Commandant admired his words
and summoned him to be an assistant.
The world called him the "Three-Word Assistant."
Wèi Jiè mocked him, saying:
"One word is enough to be summoned,
why need three?"
Ruǎn Xuānzǐ said:
"If one is the hope of all under heaven,
he can be summoned without a word,
why need even one?"
They then became friends with each other.
The *Biographies of Famous Gentlemen* states:
"Ruǎn Xiū, styled Xuānzǐ,
was from Wèishì in Chénliú.
He loved the *Laozi* and the *Yijing*,
and was skilled at expounding principles.
He disliked seeing common people,
and if he accidentally encountered them,
he would leave immediately.
Proud and without ambition,
his family had no store of grains,
yet he was content.
Wáng Chùzhòng of Lángyé, serving as the Grand Herald,
said to him:
'The Vice Grand Herald has some salary,
but you often have nothing to eat.
"Can you do it?"
Xiū said,
"Doing it is indeed possible."
Thereupon he became Grand Herald Vice-Minister,
and Erudite of the Crown Prince."
Vice-Minister of the Palace Attendants Péi married the daughter of Grand Commandant Wáng.
Three days after the wedding,
all the sons-in-law gathered for a large meeting.
*A Eulogy of the Gentlemen of the Jin* says:
"Péi Xiá, courtesy name Shūdào,
was a person from Hédōng.
His father was Wěi,
Commandant of the Changshui Battalion.
Xiá from a young age had a reputation for reason,
and was summoned as an assistant by the Minister of Works and appointed as
Vice-Minister of the Palace Attendants."
*List of Émigrés of the Yǒngjiā Era*:
"Yǎn, courtesy name Yífǔ,
his fourth daughter married Xiá."
The famous scholars of the time,
the sons and younger brothers of the Wáng and Péi families, all gathered.
Guō Zixuán was present,
and provoked Péi into a discussion.
Zixuán's talent was very rich and copious,
and at the beginning, several exchanges were not satisfying.
Guō presented his case very grandly,
Péi slowly organized the previous words,
the reasoning was extremely subtle,
The entire gathering sighed in admiration and exclaimed their pleasure.
Dèng Càn's 鄧粲 *Jìn Jì* 晉紀 [Chronicles of the Jin] says:
"Xiá 遐 made a profession of argumentation,
and was good at expounding principles of philosophy.
His diction was clear and smooth,
as pure and harmonious as zithers and lutes.
Those who heard his words,
whether they understood them or not,
could not help but admire him."
Wáng 王 also thought him remarkable
and said to everyone:
"Don't any of you try to be like him,
or you will be troubled by my daughter's husband!"
Wèi Jiè 衛玠 initially crossed the river,
and met General Wáng Dà 王大將軍.
The *Dūn Bié Zhuàn* 敦別傳 [Unofficial Biography of Dūn] says:
"Dūn 敦, styled Chùzhòng 處仲,
was from Lángyé 琅邪, Línyí 臨沂.
He was known from a young age for his understanding of principles,
and gradually rose to the position of Governor of Qīngzhōu 青州.
Seeking refuge in the south of the river,
he successively held the positions of Attendant,
Chancellor,
General,
and Governor of Yángzhōu 揚州.
He was executed for his crimes."
During a late-night gathering,
the General ordered Xiè Yòuyú 謝幼輿.
*Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Xiè Kūn, courtesy name Yòuyú,
was from Chén Commandery.
His father was Héng,
a great scholar of the Jìn dynasty.
Kūn was naturally intelligent and straightforward,
fond of the *Laozi*
and the *Yijing*,
skilled in music,
and made a profession of playing the qin and calligraphy.
He fled the disturbances to Jiangdong,
became the Prefect of Yùzhāng,
and Wáng Dūn recruited him as his Chief Clerk."
*Kūn Biézhuàn* says:
"Kūn died at the age of forty-three
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies."
Jiè met Xiè,
and was greatly pleased with him,
not even looking at Wáng again,
and they engaged in subtle discussions until dawn.
Wáng was unable to participate the whole evening.
Jiè's health was naturally weak,
and he was constantly forbidden by his mother [from such strenuous activity].
That evening he exerted himself to the extreme,
and as a result became seriously ill,
and never recovered.
*Jiè Biézhuàn* says:
"Jiè was known for his understanding of principles from a young age,
He was skilled in the *Yìjīng* and *Lǎozǐ*.
He was always burdened by illness.
Initially, he did not readily engage in external social interactions or reciprocal conversations.
His contemporary friends lamented, saying:
"When Wèi Jūn doesn't speak,
his words, when spoken, invariably grasp the truth."
In Wǔchāng, he met the Grand General Wáng Dūn.
Dūn engaged in conversation with him,
and praised him repeatedly, unable to restrain himself."
It was once said that:
